items.title: Broadcom and other AI stocks lift Wall Street closer to its record
items.description: Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are leading Wall Street higher on Tuesday, as their yo-yo moves swing back upward.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Trader Joel Lucchese works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Wednesday, Jan. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Richard Drew, file)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Richard Drew</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are leading Wall Street higher on Tuesday, as their yo-yo moves swing back upward.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are leading Wall Street higher on Tuesday, as their yo-yo moves swing back upward.

The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and pulled within 1.1 per cent of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 98 points, or 0.2 per cent, as of noon Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.3 per cent higher.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 were falling, but the gains for influential AI stocks made up for that. AI stocks are on track for a second winning day after swerving for weeks on worries about whether their boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centers and buy more AI chips.

Broadcom climbed 4.1 per cent after announcing a $63 billion financing deal where several Wall Street firms will help Anthropic get access to Broadcom’s XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions.

Elsewhere in the industry, Nvidia rose 1.3 per cent and was the only force stronger than Broadcom pushing the S&P 500 higher. CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, jumped 7.4 per cent, though it’s been careening between big gains and losses within each of the past few days.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

General Motors climbed 6.3 per cent after saying it’s moving its stock from a listing on the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq. The automaker said the Nasdaq, which is home to several of the world’s biggest technology stocks, is a fit for its tech-driven strategy. The move could also allow GM to join the Nasdaq 100 index, which would force investment funds that mimic the index to buy it.

GM began trading on the NYSE in 1911.

JetBlue Airways flew 19.6 per cent higher even though it reported a larger loss for the summer than analysts expected. CEO Joanna Geraghty said the company expects to return to making sustained operating profits next year and to deliver at least $1 in earnings per share in 2028.

Investors may have been bracing for something worse after the airline’s stock came into the day with a loss of nearly 48 per cent for the year so far.

Another travel company, Royal Caribbean Group, also helped lead the market and rose 8.1 per cent. The cruise operator delivered a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over the full year.

Companies overall are under pressure to deliver big growth in profits. Expectations are high among financial analysts and investors, and that’s what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns weighing on the market.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Boeing fell 9.2 per cent after reporting a larger loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Hilton Worldwide Holdings sank 2.8 per cent after reporting weaker revenue for the summer than analysts expected. It also gave a range as a forecast for profit in the final three months of the year whose midpoint fell below analysts’ expectations. The hotel company said it expects to see “increased impact from the Middle East” during the quarter.

Sherwin-Williams fell 1.2 per cent after delivering a weaker profit than analysts expected. High mortgage rates have helped chill the housing industry, which in turn pressures demand for the paints and coatings Sherwin-Williams sells.

“Customer sentiment and the leading indicators we track point to muted demand over the remainder of the year and into 2027,” CEO Heidi Petz said. At the same time, her company is dealing with inflation pushing up its costs for raw materials.

Confidence among U.S. shoppers has tumbled recently as pressure keeps building on them from high inflation. But a report on Tuesday said that U.S. consumer confidence improved in October, when economists expected further weakening.

In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady a day before the Federal Reserve is scheduled to announce its latest decision on interest rates. The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, but the widespread expectation on Wall Street is that it will hold rates steady this time.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.98 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Monday.

Helping to keep yields in check was a drop for oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.1 per cent to $109.48.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. Stocks jumped 3.1 per cent in Seoul and fell 1.3 per cent in Shanghai for two of the bigger moves.

AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

items.title: CTV News asked Georgia farmers about tariffs. Their answer was clear
items.description: If you ask Georgia cattle farmer Scott Craig about who has been impacted by the trade war and what costs have gone up, he’ll tell you just about everyone and everything, especially in agriculture.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Trump’s tariffs and war are delivering punishing expenses in the Deep South. Voters tell CTV News it’s testing their support.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: If you ask Georgia cattle farmer Scott Craig about who has been impacted by the trade war and what costs have gone up, he’ll tell you just about everyone and everything, especially in agriculture.
items.body:
ATLANTA — If you ask Georgia cattle farmer Scott Craig about who has been impacted by the trade war and what costs have gone up, he’ll tell you just about everyone and everything, especially in agriculture.

“I classify [it] as our three F’s. The fuel, the feed and the fertilizer.”

Craig has been a cattle farmer in McDonough, Ga., about an hour from Atlanta, for most of his life.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“I love being out here with the cows. It’s all I’ve ever done.”

But like many, he’s seen his costs go up from butchering to fuel. Beyond the import costs associated with tariffs, the war in Iran has spiked the cost of gas and diesel. One tracker published by Brown University suggests the price of diesel in Georgia has risen by US$2.18 per gallon (C$0.80 per litre) since the war began.

“It’s more than double to fill up these tractors when we either bush hog or planting or cutting hay or doing anything on them,” he said. “The cost is through the roof now.”

There is solid support for U.S. President Donald Trump in Georgia, but there are also questions about the president’s trade policy. While many are loyal to Trump, voters are divided over the high cost of living.

“I’m sure it’s going to impact people when they vote,” Craig said of the upcoming U.S. midterms.

It’s a sentiment echoed by Greg Adams, vice president at Adams-Briscoe Seed Co., a feed, seed and farm supply store in Jackson, Ga. He hopes Georgians consider Trump’s trade policies when they cast their ballots in next week’s midterm election.

“I hope it has a bigger impact than it seems. But we are down here in the South, and it’s kind of hard to see past the noise.”

Adams has noticed his costs increase too, especially for fertilizer.

“They can’t get it locally, they can’t source it locally. They have to get it from Canada, and there’s not too many other countries that are putting out the supply that y’all do,” Adams said. “My seed prices are going to go up and I’ve got to pass all that down to my customers.”

It’s not just the cost of goods coming in. Canada is Georgia’s largest export market at US$6.8 billion a year. Two-way trade between the state and Canada totalled around US$13.3 billion last year.

Georgia’s manufacturing and agriculture industries are among those in the state that have been hit hard by tariffs. The Georgia Chamber of Commerce said some businesses are delaying decisions around investment and expansion.

“The stable trade environment is what so many Georgia businesses are looking for,” said Daniela Perry, the executive director of the Georgia Chamber Foundation, the research arm of the Chamber of Commerce.

As CTV News first reported, multiple sources have said trade discussions between the U.S. and Canada have restarted in earnest ahead of the midterm elections with the U.S. keen to make a deal.

Perry hopes it happens soon.

“We want to make sure that we’re able to build those relationships at supplier networks in nations across the world, and to continue to have that predictable operations so that we’re able to create more goods and services and create better jobs for Georgians.”

items._ogDesc: Chris Smith will be Nova Scotia Power’s new president and CEO.
items.body:
Chris Smith will be Nova Scotia Power’s new president and CEO.

Smith, who is the current executive vice president of finance and commercial, is set to take the top seat on Monday, and will be replacing Vivek Sood, who took the job as CEO earlier this year.

In an announcement on Tuesday, the utility said Sood decided not to renew his contract and will work with Smith and the leadership team with Nova Scotia Power.

  • Download the CTV News App for breaking news alerts and video on all the top stories

In his time at Nova Scotia Power, Smith has served in several senior executive roles. Before that, he was the president of Heritage Gas, which is now known as Eastward Energy.

“On behalf of the Board, I’d like to thank Vivek for his leadership during a pivotal year for Nova Scotia Power, and to welcome Chris as CEO,” said Scott Balfour, chair of the Nova Scotia Power Board of Directors, in the announcement.

“Chris is a proven leader who deeply understands the business and the importance of maintaining focus on the priorities ahead. That includes supporting the new Nova Scotia Independent Energy System Operator through a complex transition in generation and system planning, while continuing Nova Scotia Power’s work to improve reliability and manage cost impacts for customers.”

items.title: UPS CEO says delivery company will make more money on slightly fewer holiday deliveries
items.description: United Parcel Service raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts on better-than-expected third-quarter earnings after cutting doorstep deliveries.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[In this March 10, 2011, a United Parcel Service driver unloads packages from a truck and arranges them for delivery in New York.(AP Photo/Mark Lennihan, File)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: United Parcel Service raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts on better-than-expected third-quarter earnings after cutting doorstep deliveries.
items.body:
United Parcel Service raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts on Tuesday on better-than-expected third-quarter earnings after cutting doorstep deliveries of millions of unprofitable packages for Amazon.

CEO Carol Tome said UPS’ focus on more lucrative business means it can make more money delivering slightly fewer packages during its critical peak holiday season quarter every year.

Shares of the world’s largest parcel delivery firm jumped nearly three per cent in early trading.

Atlanta-based UPS expects total average daily volume to be down 1.3 per cent in the fourth quarter as it becomes more selective in which packages it delivers. At the same time, executives forecast a roughly three per cent rise in revenue in the company’s domestic operation, its largest, and an estimated seven per cent increase in international revenue.

“We’re dispelling the old belief that all packages were created equal and that volume solves all problems,” Tome told Reuters.

A widening gap between the cost per parcel and revenue per parcel will improve margins, Chief Financial Officer Brian Dykes said.

UPS’ reduction in unprofitable deliveries — and the resulting lower volume reduction — in the fourth quarter means UPS can spend less on labor as well as truck and plane leases to handle the holiday package surge, Dykes said.

Tome said the outlook for holiday delivery demand is strong as US consumers continue spending despite pressures from rising inflation and prices at the pump.

“US consumers remain resilient,” she said.

Slimmer operation sets stage for growth

UPS has shuttered facilities and shed thousands of jobs after scaling back deliveries for Amazon, its largest customer. UPS said it completed the Amazon scale-down in the second quarter.

Rival FedEx, which reports results on Wednesday, is using a similar strategy. Both companies have been under pressure from investors to improve margins by focusing on higher-value shipments.

Tome also said data center construction is a significant opportunity as it touches every part of UPS, which can fly in critical components such as microprocessors, arrange ocean shipments of equipment, store goods and make final deliveries.

For the third quarter, UPS posted adjusted profit of US$1.69 per share, lower than US$1.74 per share a year ago but above analysts’ average estimate of US$1.63.

Third-quarter adjusted operating margin in UPS’ domestic unit, which generates about 65 per cent of company revenue, rose to 7 per cent from 6.4 per cent a year earlier.

The smaller but more profitable international package division also reported a higher adjusted operating margin of 14.9 per cent for the third quarter, compared with 14.8 per cent last year.

Jefferies analysts said third-quarter earnings showcased a “quarter of strong execution,” while Evercore ISI analyst Jonathan Chappell wrote in a note that the results give “some confidence in durability.”

UPS also said it was on track to meet its target of US$3 billion in cost savings this year. It has saved US$1.8 billion through September.

The company now expects 2026 adjusted profit of around US$7.28 per share, compared with the US$7.22 it had forecast in July. Analysts expect the company to report a profit of US$7.19 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG.

UPS expects annual revenue of US$92.6 billion, compared with its previous projection of US$91.2 billion and above analysts’ estimate of US$91.73 billion.

Reporting by Lisa Baertlein and Nandan Mandayam; Editing by Leroy Leo, Chizu Nomiyama, Rod Nickel and Nick Zieminski

items.title: PayPal raises 2026 profit forecast as turnaround gains traction
items.description: PayPal lifted its annual adjusted profit forecast on Tuesday, as a years-long turnaround starts to bear fruit, with improving margins and resilient consumer spending providing fresh momentum.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Signage outside PayPal's headquarters is shown in San Jose, Calif., on March 10, 2015.THE CANADIAN PRESS/AP, Jeff Chiu]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: PayPal lifted its annual adjusted profit forecast on Tuesday, as a years-long turnaround starts to bear fruit, with improving margins and resilient consumer spending providing fresh momentum.
items.body:
PayPal CEO Enrique Lores on Tuesday expressed growing confidence in the payments company’s years-long turnaround, as cost cuts and expanding margins helped drive a raise in its annual profit forecast.

The company, which became synonymous with digital payments during the pandemic, has struggled to regain investor confidence in recent years amid intensifying competition from Apple, Google and newer fintech rivals.

PayPal has laid out an extensive multi-year plan to streamline operations, cut costs and improve margins to counter these pressures and revive its share price.

  • Latest updates on company news here

“The progress we have seen reinforces our conviction in the strategy. As I look further ahead, I am increasingly confident in PayPal’s earnings growth potential,” Lores told analysts on a post-earnings call.

He took the helm earlier this year after the board ousted Alex Chriss over the pace of change and execution.

PayPal now expects full-year adjusted profit of about US$5.60 per share, compared with its previous forecast and analysts’ expectations of US$5.38, according to estimates compiled by LSEG.

The company’s shares were last up more than 1.8 per cent, reversing premarket losses. The stock is down over 80 per cent from its record high in 2021.

“What looks good is that PayPal is taking cost out much faster than expected,” Evercore ISI analysts wrote in a note.

Revival on track

The company said it was on track to achieve US$700 million in gross run-rate cost savings by the end of 2026, driven by cuts to more than 2,000 jobs and a reduction of over 25 per cent in managerial roles.

Efforts to streamline operations, optimize its portfolio and accelerate AI adoption, including using AI chat agents to support customer service, are also supporting the cost-management efforts, PayPal said.

The company has set a goal of securing at least US$1.5 billion in gross run-rate savings over the next two to three years.

Adjusted operating margin, a key metric for investors, expanded 16 basis points to 18.8 per cent in the third quarter.

Earlier this year, Reuters reported, citing sources, that PayPal had received a buyout offer of US$60.50 per share from Stripe and private equity firm Advent International, a bid that many analysts described as “low-ball.”

The offer, which valued PayPal at about US$53 billion, was reportedly deemed inadequate by the board and represented a fraction of the roughly US$360 billion valuation the company commanded at its peak in 2021.

Spending engine keeps humming

More broadly, U.S. consumers have continued to open their wallets despite economic uncertainty and sticky inflation, helping sustain spending growth across the payments industry.

PayPal’s total payment volume grew seven per cent on a foreign exchange-neutral basis to US$487.1 billion in the third quarter.

The year-end holiday season brings a crucial sales period for the payments sector, as retailers roll out eye-catching discounts and doorbuster deals online and in stores for Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Christmas.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

“We do believe that we are entering the holiday season in a better position than we were last year at this time,” Chief Financial Officer Jamie Miller told analysts.

PayPal expects adjusted profit in the fourth quarter of about US$1.43 per share, above Street expectations of US$1.35 and US$1.23 a year earlier.

For the third quarter, adjusted profit came in at US$1.45 per share, beating estimates of US$1.31.

Revenue of US$8.6 billion in the three months ended September 30 was a tad below estimates of US$8.7 billion.

Reporting by Manya Saini in Bengaluru; Editing by Sriraj Kalluvila

items.description: Hilton missed third-quarter revenue estimates and warned that U.S. midterm elections and the Middle East conflict could weigh on its performance in Q4.

items._ogDesc: Hilton missed third-quarter revenue estimates and warned that U.S. midterm elections and the Middle East conflict could weigh on its performance in Q4.
items.body:
Hilton Worldwide Holdings missed third-quarter revenue estimates on Tuesday and warned that U.S. midterm elections and the Middle East conflict could weigh on its performance in the fourth quarter, sending shares of the hotel operator down five per cent.

The latest escalation in the US-Iran war has heightened uncertainty for hotel operators and online travel agencies, overshadowing otherwise resilient leisure and business travel demand that supported spending across hotel segments, from budget accommodations to luxury stays, in the third quarter.

“Middle East is a little more beaten up than we thought,” Hilton CEO Christopher Nassetta said on a post-earnings call.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The company’s room revenue from the Middle East and Africa region dropped 5.6 per cent year-over-year in the quarter ended September 30, while for the US rose seven per cent.

Hilton, however, said it continues to grow its presence in the Middle East and Africa region, recording more than 20 hotel signing during the third quarter.

Peer Marriott’s MAR.O CEO Anthony Capuano said last month Middle East hotel revenue declines had eased in July, even as the conflict caused project delays.

Luxury strength

Hilton expects revenue per available room — which tracks average daily rate and occupancy — to grow between 4 per cent and 4.5 per cent for fiscal 2026, versus its previous forecast of a 3 per cent-3.5 per cent increase.

RevPAR at its luxury properties Waldorf Astoria and LXR rose 13.9 per cent and 14.3 per cent, respectively, during the third quarter.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Hilton forecast 2026 net unit growth (NUG) — the number of rooms added — at 6 per cent-7 per cent, on higher net room additions in the fourth quarter.

Sustained strength in Hilton’s NUG signaled higher investment in luxury brands, Jefferies analyst David Katz said.

Hilton’s quarterly adjusted per-share profit was at US$2.45, higher than US$2.11 a year ago and analysts’ average estimate of US$2.36, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Total revenue rose 6.6 per cent to US$3.33 billion, but missed the estimate of US$3.37 billion.

items.title: Boeing share price plummets with slower 737 production and free cash flow growth outlook
items.description: Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said on that the company will not reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month until early 2027.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The nose of a Boeing 737 Max airplane on the final assembly line is seen during a media tour at Boeing's factory in Renton, Wash., on April 15, 2026. (Lindsey Wasson / AP Photo)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Lindsey Wasson</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said on that the company will not reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month until early 2027.
items.body:
SEATTLE — Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said on Tuesday that the company will not reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month until early 2027, a serious setback to the company’s ongoing recovery. As a result, the company will not hit its delivery target of 500 jets this year.

The company also expects much slower free cash flow growth than investors had expected - US$3 billion next year and US$6 billion in 2028, compared to Wall Street analysts’ consensus projection of US$5.6 billion and US$9.6 billion, respectively, according to LSEG data.

Shares of the U.S. plane maker fell 9.5 per cent in early trading, reaching April 2025 lows, even as Boeing continues to recover from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The company had planned to reach 47 737 jets per month this past summer, but it will take “into early next year,” Ortberg said during an interview on CNBC.

In September, he said that Boeing has not been able to make wings fast enough.

Deliveries of the popular single-aisle jetliner are a major driver of Boeing’s cash flow.

“We are ramping up aircraft, and we’re doing that in the right way,” he said.

Before Ortberg joined Boeing in 2024, the company had struggled for years with production quality problems that were attributed to rushing rate increases at the expense of quality.

There is pressure on the company to increase 737 output faster, “but we’re going to be smart about this, stay disciplined, and the outlook is there,” Ortberg said.

The company continues to struggle with production challenges in its 787 program and 777 freighters, as first reported by Reuters on Friday.

High fuel prices have kept demand up for more fuel-efficient jetliners, but “certainly something we have to continue to watch,” Ortberg said on CNBC.

During the quarter, Boeing secured certification for the 737 MAX 7 from U.S. regulators, won the US Navy’s sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract and generated free cash flow for another quarter, while certification of the larger MAX 10 followed in October.

“Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day,” Ortberg said in a memo to employees after the results.

Boeing reported an adjusted loss of 34 cents per share for the quarter through September, compared with market expectation of 21 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Revenue at Boeing Commercial Airplanes dipped slightly to US$10.7 billion, while operating loss stood at US$697 million and margin shrank by just 6.5 per cent compared with a contraction of 48.3 per cent a year ago.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply chain.

At Boeing’s defense division, higher deliveries, improved operational performance and a US$252-million sale of a subsidiary contributed to nearly US$500 million in quarterly earnings with an operating margin of 6.2 per cent, up from 1.7 per cent a year ago.

Boeing Global Services earned US$1 billion and posted an operating margin of 18.3 per cent.

The U.S. plane maker ended the quarter with US$25.2 billion in net debt, down slightly from US$25.9 billion in the previous three months and US$30.4 billion a year ago.

Reporting by Dan Catchpole in Seattle and Shivansh Tiwary in Bengaluru; Editing by Lincoln Feast, Arun Koyyur, and Nick Zieminski

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Andrew Vaughan]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Andrew Vaughan</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Nova Scotia’s premier says the only company with rights to explore for offshore oil and gas in the province missed Monday’s deposit deadline.
items.body:
HALIFAX — Nova Scotia’s premier says the only company with rights to explore for offshore oil and gas in the province missed Monday’s deposit deadline.

Tim Houston said in a social media post Monday that Nova Scotia’s Inceptio Oil and Gas would not be able to put $50 million down as required. 

In April, regulators approved a $210-million exploration bid from the company, led by Nova Scotian James Edens, who is also president of Scotland-based Inceptio UK.

Inceptio still required an exploration licence before it could begin activities such as seismic testing and drilling. 

Houston says the lack of deposit is a setback, but the province remains committed to developing its offshore resources. 

There’s been no activity in Nova Scotia’s offshore fossil fuel sector since the Sable and Deep Panuke gas projects shut down in 2018.

“Hard things are hard but we will continue laying the groundwork for a stronger, more resilient Nova Scotia that can stand on its own and meet the challenges of tomorrow,” Houston said on social media. 

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 27, 2026.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press

Correction

This is a corrected article. A previous version incorrectly stated that Inceptio Oil and Gas was based in the U.K. In fact, the company is incorporated in Nova Scotia. While Inceptio Oil and Gas has principal shareholders in common with Inceptio Ltd. and Inceptio UK Ltd., the companies do not have ownership stakes in each another.

items.title: Canada-EU summit to kick off formal talks with Europe on closer ties: Carney
items.description: The Canada-EU Summit being held this week in Montreal will serve to launch more formal negotiations on a deeper partnership over the next year, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney is greeted by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as he arrives to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Canada-EU Summit being held this week in Montreal will serve to launch more formal negotiations on a deeper partnership over the next year, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The Canada-EU Summit being held this week in Montreal will serve to launch more formal negotiations on a deeper partnership over the next year, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday.

Carney will meet with European Union President Ursula von der Leyen and other EU officials on Thursday and Friday in Montreal, where they are expected to announce the next stage of an enhanced alliance.

“This is the launch of further formal discussions, negotiations, over the course of the next year,” Carney said on his way into the weekly cabinet meeting.

The exact nature of the new pact between Canada and the EU has been unclear — even to the leaders themselves.

In September, von der Leyen said the new arrangement could make Canada an “associate” member of the 27-member bloc. But “associate membership” does not actually exist in the EU and Canadian officials have downplayed the use of that term.

“It doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians, in terms of opportunities to study work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities,” Carney said Tuesday, adding it could open up new research opportunities as well.

Carney used the term “alliance of the future” to describe the deal, which was first made public when he spoke to the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, France, last month.

Jonathan Wilkinson, who took on the Canadian ambassadorship in Brussels earlier this year after spending more than five years in the Liberal cabinet, told The Canadian Press the labour policy discussions with Europe are focused on “specialized areas” where employers on both sides of the Atlantic could benefit from access to a shared labour pool.

He said any measures that would make it easier for workers and students to move between the two jurisdictions must be approached in a “thoughtful way.”

“We’re not talking about free movement of labour between Europe and Canada. But what we are talking about is, in some specialized areas, it may be actually interesting and useful for both countries to have the ability to tap into labour pools,” Wilkinson said.

The ambassador did not cite specific sectors where labour mobility between Canada and the EU could be eased. The EU and Canada have been discussing increased collaboration on critical minerals, technology, defence and clean energy.

Wilkinson pointed to work already done by Canada and Europe on mutual accreditation for architects and said any future decisions about labour mobility would be focused on areas of “mutual benefit.”

Michelle Rempel Garner, the Conservative immigration critic, has called on the government to explain what these negotiations mean for people coming to Canada.

“Canadians are already struggling with the cost of living due to immigration levels which are too high and have contributed to jobs becoming more scarce and workers getting paid less. Canadians deserve transparency on any EU immigration deal and how it would impact our jobs, homes, and health care,” she said in a statement.

Canada has also discussed joining Erasmus+, the European Union’s student exchange program, which offers study and training opportunities in member nations.

This week’s summit will take place on the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Canada-Europe Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA.

Nine EU members — France, Italy, Belgium, Ireland, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece and Hungary — have not yet ratified that trade deal.

Wilkinson said he’s spoken with all 27 of his EU member nation counterparts and there is momentum in Europe to get more countries behind CETA. He did not name specific nations.

“I think there are a number of countries that will be moving in that direction over the coming months. So that’s a process that will go along with the rest of this deepening of the relationship,” he said.

One of the EU’s leading nations may have a new government soon. Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is the current polling favourite to succeed Emmanuel Macron as president this spring.

Le Pen delivered a nearly hour-long speech to supporters Sunday that focused on her party’s nationalist, anti-immigrant positions.

Wilkinson said politics is always dynamic and Europeans and Canadians will go on sharing values regardless of which party is in power in a particular nation.

“I think in France, it’s a very important debate that they are having. And I think that if in fact the government were to change, people will have to take stock of that,” he said.

“But I do think that the European Union is a much bigger project than any one government in any one country. And I have a lot of confidence that Europeans will find their way through this and be just fine.”

Wilkinson said energy and critical minerals — including natural gas, hydrogen and nuclear power — will play a crucial role in the enhanced partnership between Canada and the EU.

“We’re looking at … how can we, for example, encourage significant additional European investment in Canadian minerals projects. We’re talking about how can we think about things like stockpiling together so that we actually can help to stabilize the market,” Wilkinson said.

The European Investment Bank applied for an exemption from Canadian foreign banking rules earlier this month that would allow the state investor to operate in Canada as part of a critical minerals agreement.

Wilkinson said Canada and the European Union are both looking for ways to build up the infrastructure to refine and ship critical minerals and reduce China’s market dominance.

“That’s not a dependency that’s good for Canada. That’s not a dependency good for the European Union. So we are looking at that,” he said.

items.title: Costly Construction, Decades Of Delays: Canada’s Project Leaders Get A New Playbook
items.description:
For much of the past two decades, Canada approached major projects with a simple idea: write the contract well enough, and the project would essentially look after itself. Each risk sat with a party ready to handle it, so when something went wrong, everyone knew who to turn to.

But it hasn’t worked out that way. Canada is one of the most expensive places in the world to build, and paying top dollar still doesn’t keep projects from running late (and over budget). That’s a problem at any time, but an even bigger one today, with the transportation, water, energy, natural resource, military and information technology projects currently being planned carrying multi-billion-dollar price tags — not to mention stakes in trade, sovereignty, national unity, and climate change. For developers and city-builders, these are the projects that determine where and how growth happens.

“What we’ve learned, in the last five to 10 years in particular, is that the contract is not going to save everything,” says Matti Siemiatycki, Professor of Geography and Planning, and Director of the University of Toronto’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities. “We’ve realized that contracting is really a relational business, and that the relational skills amongst the parties who are delivering the projects are central to their success.”

The reliance on contracts has roots. In the early 2000s, public-private partnerships, or P3s, became the default for major projects, and by Siemiatycki’s account, most jurisdictions set up dedicated P3 agencies (many required the model outright). He assures that P3s do have their place. They just don’t suit every project, but the industry tried to apply them to nearly everything.

This history leaves many of today’s senior project leaders in a challenging position. They came up during the P3 era with “excellent project management skills,” Siemiatycki says, “but they were trained in a world that was very adversarial.”

The Canadian Infrastructure Leadership Academy was built to help those leaders move from contract-first thinking to the relationship-driven work major projects now demand. Launched by U of T’s Infrastructure Institute at the School of Cities and the Rotman School of Management, it’s the only executive program built specifically for major project leaders in Canada. It’s designed for public and private sector leaders with 10 to 15 years of experience who are preparing to take on the largest projects in their organizations.

These industry players already know how to run a project, so the curriculum builds on that experience, with a heavy focus on leading one: building teams when several organizations share a project, understanding infrastructure as a system, rather than a linear Gantt chart, and recognizing the biases that lead projects to underestimate costs and overestimate benefits. Negotiation and conflict resolution get dedicated focus as well, “because so many of these projects end up in some form of litigation or conflict,” Siemiatycki says. Rotman’s Geoffrey Leonardelli, Professor of Organizational Behavior and Human Resource Management, brings the school’s executive leadership expertise to the faculty.

Over six months, the hybrid program combines three three-day in-person modules at Rotman in Toronto with monthly live online sessions, mentorship, a capstone project, and the chance to work through a real issue from participants’ own professional contexts.

Graduates earn a certificate from the Rotman School of Management.

Applications are open now for the inaugural cohort, which launches April 13, 2027. Siemiatycki and his team are reviewing applications as they come in, with the goal of building an intentionally diverse cohort of leaders from civil infrastructure, energy, natural resources, and industrial projects.

The program’s model has a track record abroad; the United Kingdom and Australia both run similar academies. The Canadian version is distinct, though, in that it’s shaped to suit how projects actually get built here. “If you don’t understand our culture and you don’t understand how we collaborate, the projects ultimately end up in miscommunication, and things going wrong,” Siemiatycki says. “Having the program be by Canadians, for Canadians is really important.”

When that collaboration breaks down, the companies at the table feel it. “The risk is borne by the company, especially for construction,” Siemiatycki explains. “And if it goes badly, they’re going to wear it.”

Further, the academy puts public and private sector leaders in the same room on purpose. Over six months, each side learns how the other thinks about a project, and both leave with a network to call on, if and when something goes sideways.

“Ultimately we’ll build a cohort of people that can deliver for Canada,” Siemiatycki says.

The first cohort is where that network begins. Looking forward, the plan is to grow the academy into a national program delivered locally across the country, with each new cohort adding leaders who know how to work across the public and private sides of a project. Many of the organizations Siemiatycki has spoken with already see their participation as an investment in the sector, as well as in their own teams.

As that network grows, more of the country’s major projects can be led by people who already understand how their counterparts think, and who know who to call when things get difficult. It’s the relational side of delivery Siemiatycki says the contract was never going to cover on its own.

Applications for the inaugural cohort are open now, and organizations ready to add their people to that network can nominate a member of their team to apply. Applications submitted by November 30 receive 20% off tuition.

OTTAWA — Abu Dhabi’s crown prince is in Ottawa for meetings today as Canada and the United Arab Emirates work to cement their trade ties.

Prime Minister Mark Carney will greet and participate in a welcome ceremony for Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan on Parliament Hill, before the pair take part in a signing ceremony.

Canada and the UAE concluded negotiations on a free trade agreement earlier this year in what both countries have called a “record” time of 47 days.

Carney hosted a state dinner for the crown prince in downtown Ottawa on Monday, where he said the countries’ shared determination to “build for the future” is what binds them.

The prime minister also said the leaders would share details of a strategic partnership today.

Carney visited the United Arab Emirates last November, when the UAE pledged to invest around $70 billion in Canada.

items.title: Some Canadian homebuyers tune out tariff noise as trade war rumbles on
items.description: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.content: <p>Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286291616924369.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ottawa broker says many clients are pushing ahead despite tariff uncertainty
items.body:
Geopolitical chaos and global economic uncertainty have stretched into 2026, pushing a hoped-for Canadian housing market recovery even further down the line as potential homebuyers wait for a calmer environment to emerge before making their move.

Bond market unease has sent five-year Government of Canada yields higher in recent months, pushing fixed mortgage rates upwards, while speculation is growing about at least one potential Bank of Canada rate hike in the months ahead.

Would-be buyers are still keeping a close eye on the latest political news – but while the announcement of US tariffs at the beginning of last year sent shockwaves around bond markets and hugely dented homebuyer confidence, a degree of acceptance has set in among mortgage shoppers about the trade war.

That’s according to Ottawa-based Smart Debt Mortgages broker Chris Allard (pictured top), who told Canadian Mortgage Professional many clients were still determined to push ahead with their purchase plans even with no end to the trade dispute in sight.

“I get the perception that people have largely tried to tune out some of the news and keep a positive mindset,” he said. “But there’s no doubt that everyone’s aware of what’s happening, and they’re aware that rates are rising and there’s significant concern for that.

“Now, the commentary that I often hear from borrowers, and this is true, is we see when Trump speaks now, the markets don’t automatically go up or automatically go down right away. And so that translates into the conversation that we’re having with our clients because they’re now recognizing that maybe it’s just a bunch of noise.”

Borrowers are still cognizant of the impact a big, unexpected development in the trade war would have for the economy and their plans – but they’re equally focused on making their mortgage work and optimizing their financial picture to move forward with their deal, Allard said.

“They’re trying to just look at their personal budget and try to make an educated decision based on the current environment rather than predicting if home values are up or down or rates are up or down,” he said. “They’re going, ‘What are my payments now? Am I comfortable now? And do I have a safety net?’”

BoC rate not expected to surge, even if a hike is on the way

Opinion is divided among leading economists on what’s in store from the Bank of Canada’s decision this Wednesday. Experts including Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge don’t see a hike on the way yet, although Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) now marginally expects a 25-basis-point jump.

Most of the country’s top banks expect rate hikes to arrive at some point over the next year – but none are predicting the Bank of Canada’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable mortgage rates, will hit the highs seen in 2023-24.

That’s welcome news for borrowers, according to Allard. “I think a lot of Canadians might be surprised that the banks are not projecting significant prime rate increases,” he said. “It turns out that we did see fixed rate increases – and now it looks as though there won’t be significant prime rate increases.

“So I believe that just means that we might have more clients going into variable once they start to understand that dynamic.”

Clients focus on variable amid fixed-rate rises

Allard said he’s recently noted an increase in clientele wanting variable rates with a static payment amid a wider move away from fixed rates. “Bank of Montreal [BMO] offers that, TD Bank offers that, there’s a few others that offer it,” he said.

“Borrowers are [saying] ‘Well, maybe I can benefit from a rate in the high threes, have a stable payment, even though I’m taking a variable-rate product.’ It’s a really interesting move that we’re seeing from a consumer behaviour standpoint.”

items.description: Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move
items.content: <p>Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639286370231956432.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank gears up for a massive call with experts split on its next move
items.body:
The Bank of Canada’s penultimate interest rate decision of 2026 arrives on Wednesday (October 28), and there's no consensus among experts on whether a rate hold or hike is in store.

The central bank has kept rates unchanged for nearly 12 months, with its last move in either direction arriving almost a year to the day of Wednesday’s announcement – a 25-basis-point cut on October 29, 2025.

The BoC’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable mortgage rates in Canada, has held steady since then as decisionmakers adopted a cautious approach during tense times marked by global economic uncertainty, a worsening trade dispute with the US, and inflation fears sparked by the US-Iran war.

Is a hike in store on Wednesday?

The Bank is at an “inflection point” as its next decision looms, according to Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) Economics, whose economists now say a quarter-point hike is the likeliest outcome from Wednesday’s meeting.

Still, that’s by no means a surefire thing. RBC’s Frances Donald (chief economist) and Nathan Janzen (assistant chief economist) see an almost equal probability that the BoC will hold steady this month but signal a rate hike on the way in December or January.

 Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) chief economist and senior vice president Mathieu Laberge, meanwhile, doesn’t expect a hike between now and the end of the year – but said he anticipates the BoC will begin raising interest rates at some point in 2027, potentially in the spring.

But 19 of 34 economists polled by Reuters last week see a central bank rate jump to 2.50% on Wednesday, with a majority also pencilling in a further increase before March.

The main reason for the sudden prospect of a rate hike is concern about the national inflation outlook. The consumer price index (CPI) ticked higher last month, hitting 3.1% as surging fuel prices pushed prices higher.

However, observers including National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéfane Marion believe that increase was milder than might have been expected – strengthening the case for a further rate hold.

“Core inflation is still at 2%,” Marion said during an address at last week’s Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary. “I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking [on October 28] and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

What the BoC decision will mean for mortgages

If the Bank increases rates on Wednesday, variable mortgage rates would also move higher because banks typically raise their prime rate in line with BoC moves.

Much attention will focus on the language used by BoC governor Tiff Macklem in his press conference after the announcement, with financial markets keeping a close eye on whether Macklem indicates rate increases are likely in the coming months.

As for the possible impact on the housing market of Wednesday’s decision?

A rate hold probably wouldn’t move the needle for national homebuying, which has remained sluggish through 2026 because of economic uncertainty and rising rates.

It’s unclear whether a rate hike would slow the market further, although activity has remained moribund as potential buyers stay on the sidelines even with rate increases on the horizon.

“You’d expect with lots of chatter about rate increases in Canada online bubbling through communities – plus the recent significant rise in fixed-rate mortgages in the United States – that there’d be some pull-ahead in activity,” Royal LePage president and chief executive officer Phil Soper told CMP earlier this month.

“You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs. Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat.”

items.title: Calgary's industrial market sees strongest quarterly performance since 2022
items.description: Tight supply and rising rents could boost deal flow for commercial lenders and brokers
items.content: <p>Tight supply and rising rents could boost deal flow for commercial lenders and brokers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0356_639286894738396309.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tight supply and rising rents could boost deal flow for commercial lenders and brokers
items.body:
Calgary’s industrial market tightened sharply in the third quarter, with vacancy falling to its lowest level in three years, according to a new Avison Young report.

Net absorption, the net amount of space taken up by tenants, reached 3.6 million sq. ft. That was the strongest quarterly result since Q3 2022. Total vacancy fell to 2.9%, down 1.2 percentage points from the previous quarter and down from 4.7% a year earlier.

“Robust tenant demand absorbed most newly delivered space while also reducing existing vacancies,” the report said.

Supply stays tight

The availability rate, which includes space that is vacant or will soon be, dropped to 3.5%. Sublease space is limited at 0.6%, and the report said rents are firming as competition for quality space grows.

Developers have 3.8 million sq. ft. under construction across 16 projects. About 2.0 million sq. ft., or 52%, is already preleased. Only 1.4 million sq. ft. has been delivered so far in 2026, well below the five-year average of roughly 4.3 million sq. ft.

Large-bay space is especially scarce, and the report said large-format users may need to consider design-build solutions. It also cited a shortage of development-ready, serviced industrial land, particularly within city limits.

Vacancy fell in every submarket from a year earlier. Rocky View County/Balzac saw the biggest improvement, dropping from 12.2% to 4.5%. That submarket also holds more than half of the construction pipeline, at 2.1 million sq. ft.

Capital follows demand

Industrial building investment totalled $220 million in the quarter, according to figures from The Network. That brings the year-to-date total to $861 million, about 10% above the $785 million transacted in the same period of 2025.

Among the quarter’s notable deals, Dream Industrial bought a 159,650-sq.-ft. Southeast building for $31.25 million, or $196 per sq. ft. Avison Young also brokered new direct leases of 498,000, 486,000 and 365,000 sq. ft.

Other brokerages see a similar trend, though their numbers differ because methods vary. CBRE reported 3.8 million sq. ft. of absorption and a 3.6% availability rate. It also found owner-user sale options fell 27.7% to 65. Altus Group put Calgary’s availability at 4.9%, down 140 basis points from a year earlier. It put national availability at 6.2%.

What it means for borrowers and lenders

The Avison Young report listed rising rents, normalized borrowing costs and improved liquidity among the factors strengthening development spreads. It named macroeconomic uncertainty, inflation and elevated construction costs as headwinds.

Rates remain a variable. The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% on Sept. 2. It said upside inflation risks had increased and long-term bond yields had moved higher. Its next decision is scheduled for Oct. 28.

For brokers with industrial owner-user, investor or developer clients, the data points to a market where limited options and firmer rents may affect timing and financing. The report advised tenants with upcoming lease expiries or expansion plans to start their search early.

items.title: Housing and health funding cliffs loom as federal budget nears: RBC
items.description: Federal housing funding is projected to fall from more than $10 billion to $4 billion by 2028-29
items.content: <p>Federal housing funding is projected to fall from more than $10 billion to $4 billion by 2028-29</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0356_639286892527825539.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Federal housing funding is projected to fall from more than $10 billion to $4 billion by 2028-29
items.body:
Federal housing and health funding arrangements are set to wind down in 2027-28. The coming budget could signal how Ottawa plans to replace them, according to RBC Economics.

Finance minister François-Philippe Champagne will table Budget 2026 on Nov. 5. RBC assistant chief economist Cynthia Leach said in an Oct. 26 analysis that the budget’s task is “less about new programs and more about disciplined execution.”

“Even with immediate pressures contained, two spending areas must soon be accommodated,” Leach wrote.

Housing money set to shrink

Budget 2026 could release the next version of the National Housing Strategy, which winds down in 2027-28, RBC said.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) has highlighted that federal housing funding drops from more than $10 billion in 2026-27 to $4 billion by 2028-29, even with Build Canada Homes. Recent measures, such as development charge reforms, may have lifted that profile, but they appear temporary, RBC said.

Build Canada Homes launched with $13 billion in initial funding. The PBO projects it will produce about 26,000 units and has said it is expected to add only a modest amount to housing supply. In March, Finance Canada described its full suite of housing programs as totalling roughly $40 billion.

RBC said Ottawa has responded to affordability pressures with tariff and oil-shock support for vulnerable households. It described the economy as slowly improving, with housing “sideways” in many markets.

Health transfers also expire

Several provincial health funding arrangements end in 2027-28, RBC said. They include the 5% guaranteed Canada Health Transfer escalator and one-off agreements worth about $3 billion or more a year.

Provinces are increasingly calling for a permanently higher federal share, as rising health-care costs drove deteriorating 2026 budgets, the analysis said. After a recent one-year extension of mental health funding, health minister Marjorie Michel has designated the broader issue as one for 2027.

On both files, Leach said RBC will look for efficiencies and clear, lasting terms.

“We’ll be looking for Ottawa to push for efficiencies … and for eventual agreements ideally to delineate long-term commitments rather than funding patches that punt the issue,” she wrote.

Tight fiscal room

RBC estimates $57 billion in new five-year spending commitments since the spring update, led by the $36 billion corporate tax mega deduction. It said deficits could run more than $15 billion deeper by 2030-31 than the spring update projected.

The PBO now expects a $63.3 billion deficit in 2026-27 and a balanced operating budget by 2028-29, a year later than the government promised, the Canadian Press reported. The finance minister’s spokesperson said the PBO’s assumptions differ from the government’s.

Rates add pressure. RBC noted the 10-year Government of Canada bond yield is up 40 basis points over four months. The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% in September and is scheduled to announce its next decision Oct. 28.

For brokers who work with builders, investors and affordable-rental clients, the funding timeline will affect how much federal support is available in coming years. RBC said it does not expect new funding for those areas in this budget, but it will watch how Ottawa frames the path ahead.

items.title: Sutton Group Announces Strategic Partnership With Ace Project Marketing
items.description:
Led by entrepreneur Ross McCredie, Vancouver-based Sutton Group has announced that they are partnering with Kelowna-based Ace Project Marketing, the latest move by the McCredie-led real estate company as it continues to expand its horizons.

The partnership will see Ace’s project marketing expertise and experience working with developers join forces with Sutton’s national network of over 6,000 agents in a way that the two say will benefit developers, real estate agents, and homebuyers.

As part of the partnership, Ace Project Marketing will be launching Ace Everywhere, a project marketing program designed exclusively for Sutton Group’s agents.

The firms said in a press release that the "program combines Ace’s centralized strategy, marketing and production capabilities with local agents’ market knowledge, relationships and licensed sales expertise.”

The result is Sutton agents will have support to work with presales, and Ace will bring its expertise to new markets across the country.

“For developers, the partnership brings together Ace’s insights into purchaser expectations and its sales and marketing expertise with Sutton’s national reach,” the companies said. “This collaboration offers a trusted sales and marketing pipeline, helping developers connect their projects with prospective buyers and the agents who advise them. By streamlining projects and maximizing presale success rates, the partnership supports market-driven developments and long-term success.”

“Combining Sutton’s national network of 6,000 agents with Ace’s customized market intelligence and project marketing expertise allows us to deliver data-driven solutions grounded in a people-first approach,” said Ace CEO Chad MacTavish. “Ace Everywhere gives us a practical way to grow alongside Sutton’s agents, combining the strength of a national platform with the local expertise every development needs. It reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity for Canadian housing and our commitment to building the capabilities to support it.”

Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie (left) and Ace Project Marketing CEO Chad MacTavish (right).

The Sutton Group team and Ace Project Marketing team.

“This partnership with Ace combines Sutton’s deep local roots across Canada with expertise in new housing, exactly when it’s needed most,” added Sutton Group President James Innis. “With new-home construction starts and preconstruction sales facing significant headwinds, we’re helping shape much-needed housing solutions that reflect the needs of each community, and giving our agents new ways to support buyers through a changing market.”

Sutton Group

Commenting on the partnership, Sutton Group CEO Ross McCredie called it “an exciting step forward in enhancing the services within Canadian real estate” and part of the company’s “technology-driven approach” towards delivering unparalleled value and homeowner-focused solutions for Canadians.

Sutton Group has taken several steps forward in recent years, after McCredie — through McCredie Investments — acquired the company in 2023. McCredie has spent the past few years positioning the company for long-term success in a technology-driven world and pushing the company towards a wealth-management model.

Those moves include the November 2025 acquisition of Ottawa-based real estate data technology company Homicity. With the acquisition, Homicity Co-Founder and CEO Jamie Blades joined Sutton Group as VP of Technology & Partner Success.

This spring, the company then announced a partnership with American luxury real estate brokerage Elliman (formerly known as Douglas Elliman) that would see the two companies create a new two-way referral program for their agents.

That same month, Sutton Group also announced that myAbode — an AI-driven deal processing “operating system” for residential brokerages — was making a strategic investment in Sutton Group and providing its brokerage optimization technology to Sutton’s agents.

Sutton Group has also continued to expand its footprint, opening new offices in Surrey, West Vancouver, Kelowna, Calgary, Stratford, and Gatineau-Ottawa over the past 12 months.

items._ogDesc: A Bank of Canada staff paper finds about 80% of the building boost from rate cuts comes from excess demand, and ignoring shelter inflation fuels booms.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate industry often argues the central bank should ignore shelter inflation and keep rates low to boost supply. A new Bank of Canada (BoC) staff paper tests both claims, and neither holds up as a blanket rule. The researchers find that ignoring shelter inflation during a demand-driven boom is destabilizing to the economy and pushes valuations higher. While rate cuts get more homes built, roughly 80% of that comes from excess demand created by monetary stimulus.

Housing FOMO Makes Ignoring Shelter Inflation Risky

Can the central bank safely ignore shelter inflation? Not when demand is driving it, according to the researchers. “Monetary policy should not look through shelter inflation when it is driven by housing demand shocks. Looking through creates a more volatile economy especially when faced with extrapolative expectations,” they explain.

Extrapolative expectations is a $10 term ($184.70 in 2026 dollars) for assuming a trend will continue. Home prices rise because that’s just what they do—so buyers who believe that load up on more housing and debt during a boom.

The researchers modelled a boom where home prices climb 20% over two years. Excluding shelter inflation from policy decisions pushes overvaluation as much as 2.2 percentage points higher than a policy that includes it. When buyers have rational expectations, the gap peaks around 1.3 points. In other words, trend-chasing led to a 70% larger overshoot.

“This amplifies financial stability risks, especially when price dynamics are partly driven by past increases in house prices,” warn the researchers.

Rate Cuts Are Steroids For Demand, Not A Supply Fix

Factoring shelter into rate decisions during a boom makes a hike more likely. Higher rates cool demand over time, but they immediately raise financing costs for homebuilders. Cheaper money means more building, argues the industry. In isolation, the math makes sense. Reality is a little more complicated.

“While financing costs do affect housing supply, supply-side cost effects remain quantitatively secondary to demand-driven mechanisms operating through house prices and expectations,” explain the researchers.

They modelled a 100 basis point (bp) rate cut, which lifts residential investment 6.2%. Cheaper financing accounted for just 1.4 points of that, roughly 20%. The other 80% injection comes from excess housing demand. Rate cuts technically get more homes built, but primarily by incentivizing more housing consumption.

Mortgage Interest Makes Rate Cuts Look Like Lower Inflation

After a rate cut, shelter inflation falls for about two years. That drop is mostly mechanical, as Canada includes mortgage interest costs (MIC) in CPI. Cheaper borrowing directly lowers measured shelter inflation, even though the real impact of monetary policy decisions isn’t fully reflected for 18 to 24 months. It’s a problem most countries avoid, including the United States.

Since CPI drives rate decisions and rates drive mortgage interest costs, mortgage interest creates a feedback loop. Rates fall, mortgage interest falls, measured inflation falls, and the BoC cuts rates to lift inflation back to target. The researchers call it a “policy amplification loop,” where easing reinforces the housing boom. It makes the case for ignoring mortgage interest, even as they warn against ignoring demand-driven shelter inflation.

We’ve covered this problem in depth before, so it’s nice to see it get some time in the monetary policy spotlight.

Hiking Rates Into A Supply Shock Slows Output, Not Inflation

When a supply crunch is driving shelter inflation, hiking rates barely makes a dent. Higher rates raise mortgage interest costs, offsetting much of the cooling in home prices.

Rents rise too. In the model, rental returns have to compete with what investors could earn on financial assets, so higher rates push rents up.

Responding to shelter with hikes “does little to reduce cumulative shelter inflation,” note the researchers. Total headline inflation ends up nearly identical whether the BoC reacts to shelter or not, according to the model. Economic output is a different story.

“In contrast, reacting to the housing supply shock leads to a significantly larger decline in output. This trade-off suggests that looking through housing supply shocks may be welfare-enhancing,” the researchers conclude.

Even the case for looking through shelter inflation comes with a caveat. They warn that if the supply shock persists, the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations rises, urging caution.

What The Bank of Canada’s Model Misses About Rates & Productivity

The researchers are clear: the BoC can’t safely ignore shelter inflation when demand is driving it, and rate cuts aren’t a supply strategy. Hikes restrain home prices even in a shortage, but measured shelter inflation barely moves, since higher mortgage interest costs and rents offset the cooling.

What the model doesn’t show is the cost to the rest of the economy. The study shows a 100 bp rate cut lifts residential investment 6.2%, dwarfing the boost to output and business investment. In this scenario of a housing demand shock, residential investment growth significantly outpaces the boost to business investment and economic output. The model treats this as a passing problem: one shock, and everything returns to normal within five years. That’s not reality.

The BoC doesn’t cut rates once, then take a decade off. Repeated easing has pushed residential investment’s growth past the rest of the economy, concentrating capital in housing. The model has no way for business investment to lift future productivity, the exact problem that policymakers are currently struggling with. It can’t count what’s lost when that capital is diverted from other industries, nor does it measure whether, when or how it returns. The paper shows where the stimulus goes. It just doesn’t capture the full cost.

items.title: Uniqlo to open first downtown location at Pacific Centre
items.description: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items._ogDesc: The Japanese retailer’s seventh B.C. location will join new Aritzia and Simons flagships in the former Nordstrom space
items.body:
Uniqlo will open its first downtown Vancouver store at CF Pacific Centre in spring 2027, marking the Japanese clothing retailer’s seventh location in B.C.

The Japanese retailer will join the new Aritzia and Simons flagships to take up the space formerly occupied by Nordstrom. The three stores are scheduled to open between 2027 and 2028.

“We are incredibly proud to support the growth of Uniqlo, Simons and Aritzia across Canada with these premier locations at CF Pacific Centre,” said Lillian Tummonds, senior vice-president of retail at Cadillac Fairview, which owns and operates the shopping centre, in a statement.

“This major transformation reflects our shared commitment to creating unparalleled retail destinations, and we look forward to the energy and excitement these powerhouse brands will bring to the heart of downtown Vancouver.”

Bruce Winder, a retail analyst, said the development is a "continued vote" in downtown Vancouver retail space.

"Downtown Vancouver has had a bit of a hard time getting tenants. Recently, it's been a bit of a tough sell for some brands to sign leases," Winder said.

"And they've had to deal with ... the exit of Nordstrom. Not specifically in [Pacific Centre], but Saks Fifth Avenue have left, going back, Sears left, etc. So it's been tough to fill these large boxes."

In November 2025, Vancouver-based fashion retailer Aritzia announced plans for a four-level, 40,000-square-foot flagship boutique at CF Pacific Centre, with an opening initially targeted for 2027. Cadillac Fairview's latest announcement tentatively puts the opening in 2028.

Earlier this year, Quebec-based retailer Simons announced plans to open its first downtown Vancouver store at the shopping centre. The approximately 92,000-square-foot location will span three floors and is scheduled to open in fall 2027.

Winder said several mid-sized brands have been taking up space previously occupied by a single large retailer in downtowns across Canada, including Vancouver.

Another trend he has observed in B.C. is the rise of Asian retailers as some American chains, including Target and Nordstrom, have exited Canada, alongside the closure of Saks Off Fifth stores.

"U.S. companies seem to have a harder track record, where some of the other retailers from Asia, like Uniqlo, Miniso, Muji, and some other ones, have done better in Canada," he said.

Uniqlo opened its first Canadian store at CF Toronto Eaton Centre in 2016, followed by its first B.C. location at Metropolis at Metrotown in Burnaby in 2017.

items.title: Bank of Canada now expected to hike key rate as it faces 'pivotal decision'
items.description: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items._ogDesc: Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.
items.body:
Expectations are rising that the Bank of Canada will indeed raise its benchmark interest rate this week as it considers the effect of higher energy prices on the economy.

Financial market odds for a rate hike were just over 83 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. The central bank's planned interest rate announcement on Wednesday will also include an updated monetary policy report.

The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent for seven consecutive meetings.

RBC economists said in a note to clients Thursday that they are now expecting a quarter-point hike as the central bank faces a “pivotal decision amid evolving economic conditions.”

Last week, Statistics Canada reported the annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as the war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices. Excluding gasoline, the consumer price index rose 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September, easing from 2.4 per cent in August, suggesting higher energy prices haven't significantly spread throughout the economy yet.

Meanwhile, jobs data from StatCan released earlier this month showed the labour market stalled for a second month in a row in September as the economy lost 68,000 positions.

However, the RBC economists said they have “very low conviction” on a rate hike happening this week, and see a significant chance the Bank of Canada instead uses the meeting to set up a hike in December or January.

"While we don’t see an immediate need for the BoC to hike now, at the same time, a 25-basis-point increase in the overnight rate on Wednesday won’t materially change our medium-term economic outlook compared to a December or January hike," the note reads.

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said in an interview that recent comments from Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem appeared to drive the change in expectations.

While speaking from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Macklem warned that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the inflation outlook at home.

“That essentially just emphasized that the central bank is increasingly worried about the potential impact of higher oil prices on future, broader inflation pressures, and they feel confident enough the economic backdrop is going to gradually continue to improve,” Janzen said.

The Bank of Canada released its latest business outlook survey last week, which suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter. However, it found that concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.

"All the economic data that we've had to date is consistent with the view that the central bank, the Bank of Canada, was getting closer to raising interest rates," Janzen said.

Canadian interest rates are still relatively low, he added, and the neutral range — where rates are neither helping nor hurting the economy — sits between 2.25 per cent and 3.25 per cent.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao said in an interview that it is clear the Bank of Canada is becoming more concerned about the persistence of rising energy prices, "and that's what's starting to change the calculus."

While a hike is likely, he said there are also arguments for the bank to hold its key rate.

"There's interest-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing, that are already dealing with higher bond yields and too much additional tightening risks some unnecessary weaker demand in that space," Ercolao said.

"Overall, Canada's economy is growing, but it's not necessarily overheating by any means."

The impact of U.S. trade tensions on overall investment and a weakening labour market also support a decision to hold interest rates, he said.

He said a hike on Wednesday would be a risk management measure to prevent the inflation shock from becoming more persistent.

Ercolao said higher energy prices are a double-edged sword for the domestic economy.

"On one hand, higher energy prices are good for producers and government, and corporate revenue intake. It creates higher incomes especially in commodity-producing provinces," he said.

"But at the same time, it's households especially that feel the pinch immediately from higher gasoline costs and then secondary to that, higher refined product costs end up feeding through the supply chain and into our end-user purchases."

Ercolao said that Canada has navigated the trade dispute "fairly well" by diversifying trade in certain sectors, including shipments of energy products to Asia and Europe.

"That said, there's still that acute pressure that's being placed on very reliant industries in Canada on the U.S., especially in Central Canada like Ontario and Quebec with our steel industry, our aluminum industry and our auto industry," he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press
